doc.title: Rudy Van Gelder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Worrying about equipment, tape speed and the pitch gadget
summary: He says he concentrated on whether equipment worked, and describes checking tape speed with a gadget since analog speed drifts.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, Rudy, everyone always thinks that you’re going to be able to tell all these fantastic musicians’ stories about what was going on but your concentration wasn’t on that.
No, of course not, I was totally unaware of what was going on.

I was concentrating on whether the equipment was working right, whether there was noise on channel 6, if there is a dirty contact on channel 20, whether I’m overloading the tape, is the tape running. Which period do you want talk about? Earlier on: was the tape running at the right speed? Is it going to be sharp a half a step or something? That’s what I worried about. I worry about if everything is working correctly.
And how were you able to discern if it was sharp or flat?

I have perfect pitch reading machines. I have a little gadget you never saw in your whole life. You push it against the tape and you can see the lines move forward or backward, without any kind of electronics. I can tell whether it’s working or not. I can put that at the beginning of the reel of the tape and it will show one speed, and at the end of the tape it will show another. This is true. Which is the truth. No tape machine ever ran the same speed from the beginning to the end. So the pitch would jump. I’m glad you
brought this up. Everybody says, “Oh well I like analog tape.” It’s a different speed at the end of the reel than it is at the beginning. The same thing applies to discs.
So how was that rectified or do you just live with it?
I live with it. I know about it. It’s rectified by ignorance. (Laughs)
